name: Water Intake Calculator
short: A daily water guideline from weight, training and climate. No myths.

seo.metaTitle: Water Intake Calculator: Daily Guideline, No Myths
seo.metaDescription: A weight-based daily water guideline adjusted for exercise and climate, with the eight-glasses myth retired. Honest hydration arithmetic.
keywords: how much water should i drink

intro: The eight-glasses rule is hydration's most successful piece of folklore: nobody can find its evidence, it ignores body size entirely, and it has outlived every attempt at correction. Actual guidance scales with the body doing the drinking: around 33 milliliters per kilogram per day as a baseline, more when training sweats it out, more again in real heat. An 55-kilogram person and a 100-kilogram person are not the same glass count, and no slogan survives that arithmetic.

This calculator runs the weight-based guideline with additions for exercise minutes and hot climates, and returns liters and, for the glass-minded, 250 ml glasses. It is presented as what it is: a guideline for healthy people, with thirst acknowledged as a working signal rather than the enemy, and the whole thing clearly outside medical territory, which kidney and heart conditions decisively are.
howto: Add your usual daily exercise minutes; sweat is the main variable after size.
Set the climate: hot seasons and hot countries add a real amount.
Read the daily guideline in liters and glasses.
Spread it across the day rather than dosing it; thirst plus pale-straw urine is the working check.
Count tea and coffee toward it, because physiology does, whatever the myth says.
benefits: Retiring myths is half this page's value: caffeine's diuretic effect is far too weak to un-drink a cup, so tea and coffee count; food contributes roughly a fifth of intake already; clear urine is not the goal, pale straw is; and drinking far beyond need buys bathroom trips, not detoxification, with genuine (if rare) danger at endurance-event extremes. Hydration culture has drifted into performative gallon-jugs, and a weight-scaled guideline with honest caveats is the correction.

The additions are sized from sports-medicine practice: roughly 350 ml per half hour of exercise, half a liter for genuinely hot conditions, both editable by how your body actually runs. The guideline framing is kept deliberately strict: healthy adults, ordinary conditions, thirst still respected as a signal, and medical conditions, kidney and heart above all, referred to doctors in plain words rather than fine print. Beside the [calorie calculator](/tools/calorie-calculator/) and [macro calculator](/tools/macro-calculator/), it completes the unglamorous basics that outperform every supplement aisle.

Timing advice earns a sentence because it changes adherence: a glass with each meal and one between them covers most guidelines without counting, and front-loading the day beats evening catch-up, which mostly buys interrupted sleep. Habit stacking, water attached to existing meals, is how the number becomes automatic, which is the only way any daily number survives.
useCases: Gym-goers size their intake to training days versus rest days and stop copying a training partner twice their size. People in hot summers or hot countries, Phoenix in July being the motivating example, see the climate line acknowledge what their bodies already reported. Headache-prone desk workers try the boring fix first, since mild dehydration is a documented headache trigger and the cheapest one to rule out.

Parents get sane per-weight numbers for teenagers in sports instead of marketing-driven bottle counts. And the gallon-jug crowd meets a calculator that respectfully suggests their kidneys are working hard for no prize, which some of them even believe.

faqs.a: It is unscaled folklore: fine as a vague average, wrong for most individuals. Two liters over-waters a small sedentary person and under-waters a big one training in heat. Weight-based arithmetic replaces the slogan with your number.

Yes. Caffeine's diuretic effect at normal doses is much smaller than the fluid delivered; controlled studies show caffeinated drinks hydrate nearly as well as water. The myth refuses to die, but physiology has voted.

faqs.q: Can I drink too much water?
faqs.a: Yes, though it takes effort: drinking far beyond losses dilutes blood sodium, and endurance events where people over-drink on schedule have caused genuine emergencies. The guideline plus thirst is the sane zone; forcing liters beyond it serves nothing.

faqs.q: Does food count toward the total?
faqs.a: Roughly a fifth of typical intake arrives in food, fruit and cooked meals especially. The guideline here is for drinking, with normal eating assumed; a day of dry snacks earns an extra glass, not a spreadsheet.

faqs.q: How do I know if I am drinking enough?
faqs.a: Thirst is a working signal for most healthy people, and urine color is the practical gauge: pale straw is right, dark means drink, fully clear means ease off. Two mechanical checks beat any app streak.

faqs.q: Does this apply to medical conditions?
faqs.a: No. Kidney disease, heart failure and several medications change fluid rules entirely, sometimes inverting them. That territory belongs to your doctor, and this page says so without small print.

Under an hour of ordinary exercise, water wins on every count. Beyond that, or in heavy sweat, electrolytes earn their place, sodium especially. The sugar in commercial bottles is fuel for endurance sessions and just sugar for everything else.
